newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel plans Nazareth's rebirth in the year 2000.
newsitem.headline: Israel plans Nazareth's rebirth in the year 2000.

text.p: Neglected Nazareth, the Galilee home of Jesus, is getting a new lease of life, expecting a crush of Christian pilgrims for the Vatican-proclaimed Great Jubilee in the year 2000.

Israel's largest Arab city, Nazareth is known to the world's billion or so Christians as the place where the Virgin Mary got word she would bear the son of God and where Jesus spent the better part of his life.
At home the half-Moslem, half-Christian town of 60,000 Arabs in the Jewish state is just as well known for being rundown and traffic-jammed at Christmas or any other time of year.

But those days are short-numbered, say Israeli officials, Christian clergymen and businessmen of all faiths who are praying for peace and investing in the city in hopes of enticing pilgrims for the start of the third millenium.

Pope John Paul has declared 2000 a Great Jubilee, fixing as centres for celebration the Holy Land, Rome and local churches. The Holy Land takes in Israel, Jordan and Palestinian-ruled areas including Jesus' birthplace in Bethlehem.

"It is the 2,000th anniversary of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ," said Monsignor Kamal-Hanna Bathish, in charge of Roman Catholic festivities. "It is in this Holy Land that all these mysteries that we are celebrating have taken place."

He told reporters it was hoped the Pope would visit the region for the first time since Paul VI in 1964 and a proposal was being studied for a council of world church leaders to convene in the Holy Land.
"We all hope he will be coming. Maybe not exactly in the year 2000, maybe before or after," Bathish said.

Nazareth sells itself so short that most of the one million pilgrims who visit each year spend only a few hours there and only 10 percent stay the night -- a statistic borne out by the fact the town has only 600 hotel rooms.

There are few good places to drop off pilgrims on tour buses. The main street, Paul VI, is jammed. It runs past the Basilica of the Annunciation where according to Roman Catholic tradition the angel Gabriel foretold Mary of Jesus's birth.
Tourism officials say the Vatican expects as many as 15 million pilgrims to visit the Holy Land in the year 2000.
"Nazareth is not ready and the country is not capable of absorbing so many," said tourism spokeswoman Michal Marmary. In 1995, a record year, Israel received 2.5 million tourists.

Israel expects some two million pilgrims in Nazareth alone in the year 2000. It has embarked on a plan to fix the traffic problem by the end of 1998 and build some 2,000 largely three- and four-star hotel rooms in four years.
The Old City market is getting a facelift -- a new roof and pavement. Its ugly overhead wires are being moved underground.

Ilan Oren, the Israeli tourism official in charge of "Nazareth 2000", said the government had put $94 million into a four-year project with the expectation of drawing another $400 million in private investment.
No less important than investment, however, is peace. Middle East bloodshed has hurt tourism in Nazareth as elsewhere.
"An atmosphere of tension...can have an influence for the worse," Oren told reporters.

The Israeli and Palestinian tourism ministers were due to discuss joint marketing of pilgrimage packages this week but the Palestinian, Bethlehem Mayor Elias Freij, fell ill. Palestinians complain Israeli security measures hamper their tourism.

Tourism appeared headed for a third straight record year until February and March when Palestinian Islamist suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel. An outburst of violence in September only worsened the outlook.

Israel projects a drop in 1996 tourism of four to seven percent from last year. Oren said in Nazareth alone it had fallen some 6 to 7 percent since right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu ousted Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres at the end of May.
